Not suitable for people who are poor at math, afraid of the outdoors, or unable to sit still. Hydrological modeling is inseparable from mathematics and programming, and it will be very painful if you don't have a good foundation. Going out to the wild by rivers, wells, and during flood season is normal, and it cannot be done by squeamish people.

Common paths are: Hydrology and Water Resources/Hydraulic Engineering/Geographic Information Major → Getting started in data positions at hydrological stations or consulting companies → Mastering hydrological models and programming → Taking water conservancy-related professional qualifications → Turning to hydrological forecasting, water resources management or scientific research.

It is suitable for people who have a good foundation in mathematics and science, can go into the wild, and have strong logic. Hydrology is a combination of mathematics and on-site work: the model must be calculated clearly, the field measurements must be accurate, and the results must be explained clearly; at the same time, during the flood control period, one must stay up late and stare at the data to withstand stress.

Hydrologists (Hydrologists) study the distribution, movement and quality of surface water and groundwater, and are responsible for hydrological monitoring, runoff and flood analysis, water resources evaluation, and water quality research, providing scientific basis for flood prevention and drought relief, water resources planning, and environmental protection.

paragraphs: The main theme of the day is "collection-calculation-reporting": usually at the station, we organize data, adjust models, and write reports, and regularly go to the field to maintain instruments, measure flow, and collect water samples; during the flood season, we enter a wartime state, staring at radar precipitation echoes and real-time water levels, and updating forecasts on a rolling basis to provide support for flood control discussions. The busiest months of the year are during the flood season. The rest of the time is relatively regular, with lots of business trips and outdoor activities.

In a word: monitoring, modeling, analysis, forecasting, evaluation. Specifically, it includes hydrological monitoring and field collection, establishment and operation of hydrological models, runoff and flood analysis, water resources evaluation, flood forecasting and report preparation, and water quality sampling and assessment.

AI can calculate the probability of flooding in seconds and automatically organize data, but the judgment of "whether this rain will cause a disaster and whether the monitoring data is trustworthy" still depends on people who understand water.

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show about 6,300 hydrologists employed in 2024, projected to remain at about 6,300 in 2034, a net change of 0 jobs, with roughly 500 annual openings. Median annual pay is about $92,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace hydrologists, but it will restructure the way they work: data cleaning, model calibration, and first draft reports are being greatly accelerated by AI. Machine learning and data assimilation make forecasts more accurate; however, the design of monitoring station networks, judgment of the credibility of results, on-site data verification, and flood control decision-making recommendations still require the professional experience of hydrologists.

paragraphs: 6/10 illustrates that hydrologists are a "medium to high exposure" earth science position: data processing and model calculations are being largely taken over by AI, but monitoring design, result interpretation, on-site verification and decision-making support still require professionals, and the position is being upgraded to one that can judge and make decisions.

Medium and high exposure means don’t just be a “model runner”: focus on monitoring design, field verification and decision support. AI will help you calculate, and you are responsible for “whether the calculation is correct and how to use it” - the person who makes the final decision in flood prevention decisions will always need people.

For those majoring in hydrology, water resources, and hydraulic engineering, a bachelor's degree is not enough, and a master's degree is the mainstream. During college, practice programming (Python), GIS, and field internships, don't just learn theory.

Specialize in flood forecasting, groundwater simulation, and urban flooding, and learn machine learning and digital twin tools; retain your field experience. "Understanding the field" is a rare commodity in the AI ​​era.

Water conservancy, geography, and environmental backgrounds can be transferred to hydrology: hydrology modeling and programming, with an emphasis on field data experience; the interview emphasizes mathematical foundation and flood control project experience.

The hydrology team needs an "AI + expert" combination: use AI to process data and modeling, and put experts in monitoring design and decision support; give young employees opportunities to work in the field, and don't let them only run models.
